# Citation

Meuwissen, T. H. E., Hayes, B. J., and Goddard, M. E. (2001). *Prediction of total genetic value using genome-wide dense marker maps*. Genetics. DOI: not assigned in this starter record. Source: [https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/157/4/1819/6048119](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/157/4/1819/6048119).

# One-Sentence Summary

Establishes the core genomic-selection idea: use dense genome-wide markers to predict total genetic value and select candidates before complete phenotyping.

# Scope for simitall

Use as the foundational reference for training/testing splits, genomic estimated breeding values, selection decisions, and multi-cycle gain evaluation.

# Agent-Safe Takeaways

- Prediction performance depends on the relationship between training and candidate populations.
- Genome-wide marker models can rank candidates even when individual causal loci are not identified.
- Selection workflows require explicit separation of model fitting, prediction, candidate selection, and crossing.

# Inputs to Specify

- Marker genotypes
- Training phenotypes
- Validation design and selection intensity

# Expected Outputs

- Predicted genetic values
- Prediction accuracy metrics
- Selected candidate sets

# Limitations and Guardrails

- Random train/test splits can overstate practical breeding accuracy when relatives span folds.
- Selection gain should be reported alongside inbreeding and diversity changes.

# Questions This Record Can Ground

- How should genomic-selection training and candidate populations be split?
- Which metrics should accompany genetic gain in a multi-cycle simulation?
